units.spoken: Policy Gradients: REINFORCE, Actor-Critic and PPO
Learn the move itself, judge it with a critic, and keep each update small.

Some moves cannot be scored one by one. A value method scores each move and picks the best score, which works while the move list is short. When the moves are amounts, such as how hard a robot arm pushes, there is no short list to score, and when the moves are words, the choice at each step is the next word from the model’s whole vocabulary, all the word pieces the model can write. A policy, the rule that picks the move, can be learned directly instead: the network’s scores become chances that add to one, and the model draws its next move from them. That is why this family matters now: it trains chat models to write replies people prefer, robot arms to push with the right force, and game players that must keep their moves unpredictable. The rest of this page is how it learns: REINFORCE learns once per episode, an actor-critic judges each step as it happens, and PPO reuses each batch without letting one update wreck the policy.

These methods learn the policy, the rule that picks the move, directly: a network turns the state into move probabilities, or into the action itself, and training shifts the policy toward moves that led to more reward. REINFORCE learns once per episode; actor-critic adds a critic that judges every step; PPO, proximal policy optimization, reuses each batch for several small updates. All three are on-policy: they learn from moves the current policy just made. Moves that are real numbers, such as a robot’s joint torques, are covered on the Continuous-Action Actor-Critic: TD3 and SAC page.

units.spoken: Section one, Policy-based methods

A language model is an agent that writes, one token at a time. A token is a word piece, the unit the model writes, and each token it writes is one move. The state is the prompt, the text the reply answers, plus the tokens written so far. The policy picks the next token, and the reward comes only when the reply ends. A reward model is a scorer that reads a finished reply and gives it one number for how good it is.

This is the right example because scoring every move stops working here: a value method would have to score every possible next word at each step, and the move set is not a short list. A policy method never scores every move; it learns the chances themselves, so the model draws its next token from them.

A policy-based agent skips the scores. Its network turns the state into a probability for each move, and the agent samples from them. Sampling matters when any fixed move can be beaten, as in rock-paper-scissors, where the best play is each move a third of the time.

Take a language model writing a reply to the prompt “What is the capital of France?” It picks the first token of its reply from three candidates: Paris, The and London. Replies starting with Paris score best on average (toy scores, Figure 1). That average score over the three tokens is the number training raises. The reply is “Paris is the capital of France.” Starting with The, the reply reads “The capital of France is Paris.” and scores in the middle; starting with London, it reads “London is the capital of France.” and scores lowest. The reward here is a reward model’s score of the finished reply. Two scores matter here: the score for one token, and one reply’s score. The number that shrinks later rewards is 1 inside one reply: later rewards in the same reply are not shrunk.

Take a look at this figure. One draw is noisy: it pushes its own token up and the others down, so a single sample can lift a token that scored badly. The average over many draws is steadier, because each row is weighted by how often its token is drawn. Paris is drawn most and scores best, so the average push points up for Paris and down for The and London, and that average is the direction training follows, not any one row.

Figure 1 shows the push behind the policy gradient: each draw pushes its own chance up and the others down, so over many draws the policy moves toward the tokens that score best. What the reader gets is the bold row at the bottom: it is the direction training takes, up for Paris and down for The and London, and it is the direction that raises J. Take a draw of Paris: the top row pushes Paris up and the others down, the rows below follow the same order, and the average of many such rows is the gradient.

Equation 1. A language model writing a reply picks each token by chance, so the way to raise its score is to push the tokens it samples. A rock-paper-scissors player who must mix moves to stay unbeaten needs the same kind of push.
Take a look at this equation. Five lines build the gradient.

Raw scores cannot be drawn from, so each score is made positive and divided by the total over all three tokens. The result is a share of one whole, so the three chances add to one and the model can draw its next token from them. The highest score gets the largest share, yet the others keep some chance.
Intuition. This line is a fraction, the softmax: the top holds one token's score made positive, the bottom adds that positive score over every candidate token.
Example. Take the three first tokens: Paris scores highest, so its chance is largest, yet The and London keep some chance and can still be drawn.

J is one number for the prompt: the average score the policy earns here. Each token's score counts in proportion to how often the policy writes it, and each term multiplies the token's chance by its score, so raising J means shifting chance toward the tokens that score best. Paris counts most, London least.
Intuition. This line is a sum over the three tokens, each term a chance times a score.
Example. Take the three tokens: Paris's best score counts most, London's lowest least.

A push on a chance cannot be carried by one drawn token directly, so the log turns it into a push divided by the chance. A token sampled often is pushed a little each time, while a rare token gets one large push, and the size and the frequency cancel, so every token is pushed fairly.
Intuition. This line is a fraction too: the change in a token's chance on top, the chance itself below.
Example. Take London, rarely drawn: its chance is small, so the one time it is drawn its push is large, matching the many small pushes on Paris.

This line names the direction training takes: how the policy's quality changes as the weights change. It is the gradient of J, the chance-weighted average score, with the scores held fixed. The equals sign promises the change written as an average over the tokens the policy samples, and only the chances move.
Intuition. This line and the next are one equation: a name and an equals sign here, the sum on the next line.
Example. Take the prompt 'What is the capital of France?': the direction that raises J is the average push over Paris, The and London, weighted by their chances, up for Paris and down for London.

The direction is a sum over all three tokens, each term a chance times a log push times a score. The chance times the log push in each term is the plain push, so the sum is an average over sampled tokens. One drawn token's push, weighted by its score, is a fair sample of the direction.
Example. Take many draws: Paris is drawn most often, and the average of those pushes over many draws is the direction that raises J, the bold row of Figure 1.
The first step is REINFORCE: the simplest way to learn a policy, from whole episodes, then steadying it.
REINFORCE, the simplest policy-based method, learns once per episode. After one reply, REINFORCE pushes the token it sampled by the reply’s score (Figure 2).

Learning once per episode is the simplest thing a policy method can do, and the noisiest: one reply’s score judges every token in it, good and bad alike, so a token that happened to sit in a good reply gets pushed up whether it earned it or not.
That noise has a cost: a token drawn early gains chance, gets drawn more, and gains more, so a run, one training from the starting chances, can lock onto a worse token.

What this figure is teaching is that one reply can mislead. The reply starts with The and scores well, so The rises toward Paris even though Paris scores best on average. Every token in that reply is pushed up by the same score, good and bad alike, so a token that happened to sit in a good reply gains chance it did not earn. That is the noise REINFORCE pays for: judging every token by one reply's score. A run can lock onto The from one lucky reply.

Figure 2 shows one REINFORCE update: the token chances before and after a reply that starts with The and scores well. The bars on the left are the chances before the update, most on Paris and least on London, and the bars on the right are the chances after, with The risen toward Paris and London fallen a little. Take the sampled token The: the update pushes it up by the reply’s score, so its bar grows while London’s shrinks. That rise is noise: one reply’s score judges every token in it.

Equation 2. REINFORCE learns once per episode, with no judge for single steps, so it needs one loss that turns a finished reply into a push on every token in it. A coach who scores a player only on the final result has only that one number to work with.
Take a look at this equation. One loss pushes each token.

The loss adds up every step's log chance weighted by the return from that step on, with a minus in front. The sum runs over the reply's tokens, and the minus turns a raise into a loss, so minimizing it pushes each token up by its return. A reply that scores best pushes its tokens up the most.
Intuition. This line turns a whole finished reply into one number to minimize.
Example. Take a reply that starts with Paris and scores best: its tokens are pushed up the most, since the reply's score weights every one of them.
One REINFORCE episode on CartPole, the smallest control problem here, from gymnasium, a library of test environments: two moves, push the cart left or right to keep the pole up.
This code plays one REINFORCE episode on CartPole.

1. Sets the number that shrinks later rewards to 0.99, opens CartPole, and builds a small policy network with Adam, an optimizer that adjusts each weight’s step from its past gradients, at a learning rate of 0.01.
2. Plays one full episode, keeping each move’s log-probability and reward. Categorical turns the scores into chances to draw from.
3. Computes the return from each step on, backward from the last reward.
4. The loss from the REINFORCE equation card, then one gradient step.

Its weakness is noise: the return from step t on includes the luck of every later reward, so updates vary a lot between episodes (Sutton and Barto, chapter 13). Subtract what the state usually returns, the average score, and the push keeps its direction with far smaller swings (Figure 3).
A baseline is the usual return from this state, the score the reply usually gets, so each token is judged against the usual, not zero.

Here is the point of this figure. Without a baseline the pushes on Paris swing widely, because each one depends on which token happened to be drawn. With the baseline taken off, the pushes cluster tightly around the same average rise. The average does not move: subtracting the usual return changes nothing on average, since the chances always add to one. What changes is the spread, and a tighter spread is steadier learning from the same replies. The baseline buys steadiness without changing the direction.
Figure 3 shows why the baseline matters: without it the pushes swing widely, with it they cluster tightly around the same average rise.

Equation 3. One reply is a noisy judge of a token, so each token needs judging against what its state usually returns. A coach who scores a player against the team's usual result compares each play with the usual.
Take a look at this equation. The advantage replaces the return.

The advantage is one reply's score minus the usual return from its state. A token that beats the usual gets a positive edge and is pushed up, one that falls short gets a negative edge and is pushed down. Paris beats the usual by the most, The falls just short, and London falls furthest short.
Example. Take a reply starting with Paris, the best on average: its return beats the usual return, so its advantage is positive.

The loss is the REINFORCE loss with one change: the advantage in place of the return. Only the weight changes, so the push follows the edge over the usual, not the raw score. A token that beat the guess is pushed up, one that fell short is pushed down, and the average push stays the same.
Intuition. The advantage must reach every token in the reply, so the push follows the edge over the usual, not the raw score.
Example. Take a reply starting with London that falls short of the usual return: its advantage is negative, so London is pushed down.

A baseline shared by every token changes nothing on average: it pushes Paris, The and London by the same amount, and the chances always add to one, so those pushes cancel to zero. The average push stays the same as REINFORCE without a baseline, with far less noise.

Each reply’s score is its token’s score plus some noise. With no baseline every score here is above 0, so whichever token is drawn gets pushed up. A token drawn a few times early gains chance, gets drawn more and gains more, so over many replies a run can lock onto a worse token. Subtracting the baseline keeps the average push but sets how far separate runs drift apart: they agree most when the baseline sits near the state’s average score before any update, while a baseline far above the state’s average score lets them drift almost as far as with no baseline, with almost every push down instead of up.

Take a look at this figure. With the baseline set to the usual return, each token is judged against the usual instead of against zero. Paris sits above zero, The just below, London further below, so the advantages spread around zero instead of clustering on one side. That spread is the payoff: a token is pushed up only when it beats the usual, and pushed down when it falls short, so separate runs agree instead of drifting apart. The baseline that does this best sits near the usual return itself.

Figure 4 shows the payoff of setting the baseline to J: with the baseline set to J, each token is judged against the usual return. Each dot is one token's advantage, its score minus J: Paris’s sits above zero, The’s just below, London’s further below, so the dots spread around zero instead of clustering on one side. Take the reply starting with The: its advantage sits just below zero, so that token is pushed down a little, and separate runs end close together.

What this picture is teaching is that noise shows up as spread between runs. With no baseline the twenty runs end far apart, some locking onto The and some onto Paris. With the baseline set to the usual return the runs end close together and high. The lesson is not that one run was lucky: it is that the baseline narrows where runs end, and narrow endings are steadier learning. Judge the baseline by the spread of endings, not by any single run.

Press the button that sets the baseline to the usual return, then step through the replies and watch the bold run. It ends high with the baseline set, and low without it, while most runs end high either way. One run can mislead, and the spread across runs is the truth.

Figure 5 shows the baseline demo: the bars give each first token's chance after the picked reply, and the spread of curves shows Paris’s chance over many replies. The top slider sets the baseline b, and the button below it sets b to J, while the lower slider steps through the replies, from the starting chances to reply sixty. The dark bar is the drawn token, its arrow A showing the push; the bold curve is one of the twenty runs the demo plays, and the bars are that run’s chances after the picked reply. Take the demo at rest, with no baseline: “The” is drawn at 0.95, arrow up, while the bold run ends low and most runs end high.
A policy that puts almost all its chance on one token stops trying the others (Figure 6).
Early draws push one token up, it gets drawn more, and the policy stops sampling the others before it has learned which is best.

Here is what to take from this figure. Entropy measures how undecided the policy still is, and the three spreads show the range. Even shares carry the most entropy, uneven shares carry less, and giving everything to one token carries none. A policy that has decided stops trying the others, so the danger is deciding before the evidence is in. Keeping the chances spread out while learning is young is what keeps the options open. The entropy bonus in the loss is the price of deciding too early.

Figure 6 shows three ways to spread chance over three tokens, and how spread out each one is, measured in nats, the unit of entropy when the log is natural: uneven, even, and certain. The left bars share chance unevenly and carry middling entropy, the middle bars give a third each and carry the most, and the right bar gives everything to one token and carries no entropy. Take the even spread: each token holds a third of the chance, so the policy stays most undecided and its entropy is the highest of the three.

Equation 4. A policy that puts almost all its chance on one token stops trying the others, and a reply that locks in too early never finds a better one. A player who only ever tries one opening is caught in the same trap.
Take a look at this equation. The loss rewards staying undecided.

Entropy adds up each token's chance times the log of that chance, with a minus in front. Each log is below zero for any chance under one, so the minus makes it positive. It is largest when the three tokens share chance equally and zero when one token takes it all, so it measures how undecided the policy still is.
Example. Take Paris, The and London sharing chance equally: each term is the same and the entropy is at its largest.

The total loss is the baseline loss minus a small weight times the entropy. The loss term is the baseline loss the advantage equation already built, and beta is the small weight on the bonus. Locking onto one token too early loses the bonus, so staying spread out costs less than deciding before the evidence is in.
Intuition. The loss rewards the policy for staying undecided, so locking onto one token too early costs more than keeping the options open.
Example. Take a reply where Paris gets almost all the chance and The and London almost none: its entropy is near zero, so the bonus is small.
One point one, REINFORCE in practice

This table is the REINFORCE runbook. Find a setting in the first column and read across for what raising or lowering it does and the value the example uses. Read the gotchas row before running the code.

Table 1 gathers how REINFORCE runs in practice: once per episode, with the policy network alone, and one backward pass over the episode. Each row names one part of the run: the setting rows say what raising or lowering it does and which value the example code uses, and the rest name the setup, the code, and the pitfalls. Take the learning-rate row: raising it learns faster until the scores climb without bound instead of settling, while lowering it steadies the run but slows it down.

A value method scores each move and picks the best, but needs a short move list. REINFORCE learns the chances from whole episodes, so it works where the moves are words, but pays in noise and in waiting.
Section two, Actor-critic methods
The second step is actor-critic: judging each move one step later instead of waiting for the episode to end.
Waiting for the end of an episode to judge every move is slow and noisy. An actor-critic agent judges each move one step later, by whether things went better or worse than it expected.

In actor-critic, the actor is the REINFORCE policy. The critic is a learned baseline that estimates the return from a state. Scoring both the state before and the state after a move lets it judge that move one step later, not at the episode’s end (the same chapter 13). After the token The, the critic’s guess for the rest of the reply drops; that drop judges the token now (Figure 7). That drop is the TD error: TD stands for temporal difference, the difference between two guesses a step apart.
The one-step surprise is only as good as the critic’s guesses, so a wrong critic misjudges moves.

Take a look at this figure. One step carries two lessons at once. The critic's guess falls after The, so the surprise is negative, and that one number trains both halves: it pushes the actor away from The, and it pulls the critic's earlier guess down toward the new lower one. The actor and the critic learn from the same step, from the same surprise, and that sharing is what makes actor-critic fast. A wrong critic misjudges, so the speed is only as good as the guesses.

Figure 7 shows one step through the actor and the critic: the actor picks The, and the world returns no reward and a next state the critic values lower. The critic's guess falls after The, so delta is negative, and the purple arrows carry that delta up to the actor and around in a loop to the critic itself, training both from the one step. Take the token The: the guess falls, delta is negative, and the actor's chance of The is pushed down while the critic's guess for the earlier state is pulled down.

Equation 5. Waiting for a whole reply to judge one token is slow and noisy, so the critic's guess replaces the wait. A coach who judges a move from the position it reaches, instead of the final result, judges without waiting for the end.
Take a look at this equation. One surprise trains both.

The advantage is the average return of one move minus the critic's guess for its state. A move that beats the guess is worth more than expected, so it is pushed up, and one that falls short is pushed down. The is worse than expected, since its reply scores less than the critic guessed, so its advantage is negative.
Example. Take the token The: its reply scores less than the critic guessed, so its advantage is negative.

Delta is the one-step surprise: one real reward plus the next state's discounted guess, minus this state's guess. It estimates the advantage rather than equaling it, since the critic's guess stands in for the truth. When the guess falls after a move, the surprise is negative, and the wait for the whole reply is gone.
Intuition. The critic's guess can judge a move one step later, so the wait for the whole reply is gone.
Example. Take the step after The: the guess for the rest of the reply falls, so the surprise is negative and the estimate says The did worse than expected.

The actor loss is minus the log chance of the move times the advantage. The log takes the chance the policy gave the move, and the advantage multiplies it, here the one-step surprise. The minus turns a raise into a loss to minimize, so the move grows likelier only when it beat the guess.
Intuition. The actor learns from the surprise alone, so this line pushes the move by how much it beat the guess.
Example. Take the token The with its negative surprise: the actor loss pushes The down, so it grows less likely next time.

The critic loss is the same surprise squared, so a miss either way counts. The brackets hold the one-step surprise, and the power of two outside squares the gap. Shrinking it pulls the guess toward the new lower one, so the critic learns from the same step that trains the actor.
Intuition. This line is the same surprise in brackets, squared.
Example. Take the guess for the state before The: the critic loss pulls it down toward the new lower guess, so the next guess starts closer.
One surprise trains both halves: the actor loss pushes the move by how much it beat the guess, and the critic loss pulls the guess toward the new lower one.
One update on the last batch of steps the current policy played, the batch size in steps, where no grad stops gradients flowing through the next-state guess and holds the next state’s guess fixed.
This code runs one actor-critic update on a batch.
1. Critic values and the one-step surprise, from the equation card in Section 2.
2. Actor loss with the advantage set to the one-step surprise, detached so it trains only the actor, the up arrow in Figure 7.
3. Critic loss, the loop in Figure 7 that trains the critic.
4. One gradient step on both losses.

A3C, asynchronous advantage actor-critic, runs many workers on copies of the world, all updating one shared network, and uses a return over a few real rewards before the critic’s guess takes over (Figure 8), with the entropy bonus. A2C, advantage actor-critic, is the synchronous version: all copies step, then make one joint update.

The return over a few real rewards is the middle ground: one real reward plus the critic’s guess is fast but leans on the critic, while the whole episode’s return is true but slow and noisy. A few real rewards plus the guess splits the difference, and how many sets where the split falls.

What this figure is teaching is that the n-step return is a middle ground, not a compromise without a reason. One real reward plus the critic's guess is fast but leans on the critic, while the whole episode's return is true but slow and noisy. Adding more real rewards before the guess takes over trusts the critic less and waits longer. The number of real rewards sets where that split falls. With one real reward the split sits at the critic, and with a whole episode at the truth.

Figure 8 shows the n-step return. The boxes add the first rewards one by one, each shrunk by gamma, and the last box is the critic's guess at the far state, so the bracket below holds the whole return. Take the return with three real rewards: it adds the first three rewards, each shrunk by gamma, and then the critic's guess for the rest.
Two point one, A3C and A2C in practice

This table is the A3C and A2C runbook. Start from the workers row: more copies of the world feed the shared network more varied experience at more CPU. The other rows set the return length and the learning rate.

Table 2 gathers how A3C and A2C run in practice: workers updating a shared network, each after a few actions or at an episode's end. Take the workers row: more copies of the world feed the shared network more varied experience, at the cost of more CPU.
Section three, PPO clipping
The third step is Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO): reusing each batch for several updates while keeping every update small.

A batch of steps only describes the policy that played it, so learning from it several times is safe only while the policy stays close to that one. PPO reuses one batch of replies for several updates, but stops rewarding once a token’s chance has moved too far from where the batch was collected (Figure 9).
One batch of replies is expensive to collect, so each one should teach as much as possible.

The ratio is the new chance divided by the old chance for the same move, so it says how far the policy has moved since the batch was collected. Above 1 the move grew more likely, below 1 less likely, at 1 unchanged.

Here is the point of this figure. The band is symmetric, but what it does is not. Past the edge on the helpful side, pushing Paris further earns nothing, because the objective goes flat and the extra change stops counting. On the harmful side the line keeps moving, so a change that hurts still counts in full. The clip lets good moves grow only this far, and never lets a bad move hide behind the same limit. That one-sided effect is the whole safety of PPO.

Figure 9 shows the clipped objective in two panels: the top for a move with a positive advantage, the bottom for a negative one. In each panel the dashed line is the unclipped objective and the solid line follows it inside the band from 0.8 to 1.2; past the edge on the helpful side the solid line goes flat, while on the harmful side it keeps moving. Take Paris: past the ratio 1.2 its line goes flat and the change counts at the edge, while The, scored badly and made more likely, keeps counting in full.
PPO is actor-critic. Without that stop, every extra pass pushes the same moves further using advantages measured under the old policy, the new policy drifts far from it, and performance can collapse:
Equation 6. PPO is also the RL step of RLHF, reinforcement learning from human feedback. A trainer who caps how far one session may move an athlete sets the same kind of limit.
Take a look at this equation. Three lines bound the policy.

The ratio is the new chance divided by the old chance for the same move. Above one the move grew likelier, below one less likely, and at one it is exactly as likely, unchanged. The ratio says how far the policy has moved since the batch was collected.
Intuition. This line is a fraction: the new chance on top, the old chance below.
Example. Take the token Paris: the new policy gives it more chance than the old one did, so its ratio sits above 1.

Clipping holds the ratio inside a band around one. Epsilon is the band's half-width, so the band runs from one minus epsilon to one plus epsilon. A ratio inside comes out unchanged, one past the top comes out as the top, so a move past the edge stops counting any further.
Example. Take the token Paris: with a ratio inside the band it comes out unchanged, and pushed past the top it comes out as the top.

The objective takes the smaller of the plain term and the clipped term. Paris past the edge with a positive advantage counts at the edge, while The counts in full. Pushing a move further past the band earns nothing, while a change that hurts still counts in full, so the update takes the safer of the two.
Intuition. This line takes the smaller of two terms at every step.
Example. Take the token Paris, which the new policy favors far more, with a positive advantage: its ratio sits past the top of the band, so the clipped term counts it at the edge.
Take Paris: pushed past the edge, it would keep gaining chance on every pass until the model only ever starts replies with Paris.

One PPO update over a rollout, the steps just played, from CleanRL, a library of single-file example implementations, with EPOCHS passes over shuffled minibatches, small slices of the rollout used for one update each. The snippet shows the policy half only: it trains the actor on the clipped objective. The critic trains beside it on its value loss, half the squared error of its guess against the returns, the advantages plus the values, clipped like the objective, and CleanRL trains both halves together in one combined loss:
This code runs one PPO update over a rollout.
1. Freezes old log-probabilities and advantages by detaching them; loops over epochs and minibatches.
2. Ratio, the ratio line on the equation card in Section 3: exp of a difference of logs is the ratio of the chances. Categorical turns the actor’s scores into chances to draw from, as in Section 1.
3. Clip, the clip line, the band in Figure 9.
4. Objective, the objective line, turned into a loss.
5. One gradient step per minibatch.
PPO gets the advantage from GAE, generalized advantage estimation. How PPO fits the alignment step is covered in Aligning Language Models with RL.

GAE adds up the one-step surprise at each step ahead, weighted by the blend weight raised to how far ahead it is, so near steps count most. With the blend weight at 0 only the first surprise counts; with the blend weight at 1 the blend is the full return minus the critic’s guess.
Three point one, PPO in practice

This table is the PPO runbook, the longest of the three. Read it by setting: the clip row sets the band, the K row sets how many passes each batch gets, and the GAE lambda row sets how fast later steps fade.

Table 3 gathers how PPO runs in practice: copies playing steps, then passes over minibatches of the rollout. The settings above are CleanRL's ppo.py settings for CartPole. The same library also runs PPO on MuJoCo, a simulated-robot task, and on Atari, classic video games, with different settings for each.
PPO is the RL step of RLHF, the step that turns a text predictor into a helpful assistant, and the clip is what makes that step safe to repeat.
When the move is a real number, such as a joint torque, there is no list of chances to push. The actor-critic idea for real-number moves is on the Continuous-Action Actor-Critic: TD3 and SAC page.
